title: Conditionals
intro: This unit adds **if**. Turkish has one suffix for it, `-sA`, with the type II endings you know from the past tense ([A2 unit 1](gp-person-endings-types)): *gelsem*. Straight on the verb stem, it imagines, wonders and suggests. After a tense, as `-(y)sA`, it makes the everyday real **if**: *gelirsem*, *geliyorsan*, *geldiyse*, and nouns take it too: *hastaysan*, *varsa*. A question word with it gives **whenever** and **whatever**, and a few set patterns turn it into advice.

blocks.text: The conditional suffix `-sA` goes straight on the verb stem. It has two-way harmony and takes the type II endings of the past: *-m, -n*, nothing, *-k, -nIz, -lAr*. Because it starts with a consonant, stems never change before it: *gitsem*, *etsem*, *yesem*, *desem*.

blocks.title: *gelmek*: if I came, if I were to come

rows.en: if he or she didn't come
if you didn't come (plural or polite)
Should you come? (Maybe you should come.)

blocks.caption: Four more verbs: no stem changes before `-sA`
head: Verb
If I…
If I didn't…
Should I…?

blocks.text: The question particle *mI* comes after the personal ending, as in the past: *gelsem mi?* like *geldim mi?*

**A hypothesis.** With the aorist in the main clause, `-sA` sets up an imagined case, one you don't really expect: *Param olsa bu evi alırım* (If I had the money, I'd buy this house), *Erken yatsan bu kadar yorulmazsın* (If you went to bed early, you wouldn't get so tired). For a condition you do expect, use the real conditional of the next section.

**Should I?** In a question, `-sA` wonders what to do, often with *acaba* (I wonder): *Gitsem mi?* (Should I go?), *Ona söylesem mi acaba?* (I wonder if I should tell her). With a question word: *Ne yapsam?* (What should I do?), *Kime sorsam?* (Who should I ask?). The last section of this guide has more ways to suggest and advise.

items.en: If I had the money, I'd buy this house.
If you went to bed early, you wouldn't get so tired.
Should I go or not?
What should I do?
I wonder if I should tell her.

blocks.text: `-sA` alone carries no tense. *Yarın gelirsen sevinirim* (If you come tomorrow, I'll be glad) is an ordinary plan; *Yarın gelsen sevinirim* is softer, almost a wish: **I'd love it if you came tomorrow**.
With `-(I)rdI` in the main clause, `-sA` makes the **unreal** conditional: *Zengin olsam dünyayı gezerdim* (If I were rich, I'd travel the world). It comes in [B2 unit 1](gp-unreal-present).

For an ordinary **if**, a condition that may well be true, Turkish puts `-(y)sA` after a tense, just as it puts `-(y)DI` after a tense in [B1 unit 1](gp-di-compounds). The personal ending comes last and is type II: *gel-ir-se-m*. The y appears only after a vowel: *gel-di-y-se*, *hasta-y-sa*.

rows.en: if he or she doesn't come
if you don't come (plural or polite)

blocks.text: **They.** In the third person plural *-lAr* usually comes before the conditional: *gelirlerse*, *gelmezlerse*, *geliyorlarsa*. *Gelirseler* is also correct.

**No question form.** A condition is not itself questioned. The question goes on the main verb: *Gelirsem kızar mısın?* (Will you be cross if I come?), *Yağmur yağarsa ne yapacağız?* (What will we do if it rains?).

If I…
Meaning

if I'm coming; if it's true that I come

blocks.text: **Which tense?** For a condition about the future, the aorist is the usual choice: *Yarın yağmur yağarsa evde kalırız* (If it rains tomorrow, we'll stay home). The other tenses keep their own meaning: *geliyorsan* is **if you're coming** (now, or as planned), *geldiyse* **if he has come** or **if he came**, *geleceksen* **if you're going to come**, and *gelmişse* **if he has come**, from what you've heard or can see.
**The past.** The standard form puts `-(y)sA` after the past and the ending last: *geldiysem*, *geldiysen*. In speech you will also hear the ending before `-sA`: *geldimse*, *geldinse*, *geldikse*.

**The main clause** comes second, usually in the aorist, the future, the imperative or the optative: *Geleceksen haber ver* (If you're going to come, let me know), *Ali geldiyse başlayalım* (If Ali has arrived, let's start).

**Nouns and adjectives** take `-(y)sA` directly, as they take `-(y)DI`: *hastaysan* (if you're ill), *evdeyse* (if she's at home), *yorgunsanız* (if you're tired). *Var* and *yok* give *varsa* and *yoksa*, and *değil* gives *değilse*: *Vaktin varsa bir kahve içelim* (If you have time, let's have a coffee), *Sorun yoksa yarın gelirim* (If there's no problem, I'll come tomorrow).

head: Word
With `-(y)sA`
Meaning
rows: if he or she is at home

blocks.text: **Varsa or olursa?** *Vaktin varsa* is about now. For a later time, use the aorist of *olmak*: *Yarın vaktin olursa bize gel* (If you have time tomorrow, come over).

**Yoksa.** At the start of a clause, *yoksa* means **otherwise, or else**: *Acele et, yoksa treni kaçıracağız* (Hurry up, or we'll miss the train). In a question it offers the other choice, **or**: *Çay mı içersin, yoksa kahve mi?*

items.en: If it rains tomorrow, we'll stay home.
If you're going to come, let me know.
If Ali has arrived, let's start.

items.tr: Bu filmi izlemediysen bu akşam izleyelim.
items.seg: Bu filmi izle|me|di|y|se|n bu akşam izleyelim.
items.en: If you haven't seen this film, let's watch it tonight.
If you're ill, stay home.
If you have time, let's have a coffee.

blocks.text: English uses the present after **if** for a future condition (**if it rains tomorrow**); Turkish uses the aorist, *yağarsa*, not the future. *Yağacaksa* means **if it's going to rain**: a forecast you've heard, or a plan.
Harmony follows the last vowel of the whole word, so after *-yor* it is always *-sa*: *geliyorsa*, *gülüyorsa*. The past keeps its own vowel before the y: *geldiyse*, *okuduysa*, *gördüyse*.

blocks.title: Spelling
blocks.text: The conditional is written as one word with what it follows: *gelirse*, *hastaysa*. Formal and older texts sometimes write it apart as *ise*: *hasta ise*, *gelir ise*.

sections.title: Eğer, ya, and ne zaman istersen

blocks.text: **Eğer** (if) can open a conditional clause, but the verb still needs its conditional ending: *Eğer yarın yağmur yağarsa evde kalırız*. *Eğer* adds nothing to the meaning. It warns early that a condition is coming, which helps in a long sentence and in careful speech.

**Question word + -sA.** With a question word and a verb like *istemek* (to want), the conditional means **whenever, wherever, whatever**: *Ne zaman istersen gel* (Come whenever you want), *Ne istersen al* (Take whatever you want), *Kim isterse gelebilir* (Anyone who wants to can come). The main clause often picks the question word up again: *Nereye istersen oraya gideriz* (We'll go wherever you want).

head: Question word
With `-sA`
Meaning
rows: however you want, as you like

blocks.text: *Nasıl istersen* (As you like) is also a reply on its own, often with *fark etmez* (it doesn't matter): *Pizza mı, kebap mı? — Nasıl istersen, benim için fark etmez.*
**What if?** *Ya* at the start of a conditional clause asks **what if**, and the rest is left unsaid: *Ya yağmur yağarsa?* (What if it rains?), *Ya otobüs gelmezse?* (What if the bus doesn't come?).
**In that case.** A condition that has just been named is picked up with *o zaman* (then, in that case) or *bu durumda* (in this case): *Yağmur yağarsa ne yaparız? — O zaman sinemaya gideriz.*

items.tr: Eğer yarın vaktin olursa bize gel.
items.seg: Eğer yarın vaktin ol|ur|sa bize gel.
items.en: If you have time tomorrow, come over to our place.
Come whenever you want.
We'll go wherever you want.
Take whichever one you want.
What if the bus doesn't come?

blocks.text: *Eğer* never replaces the suffix: *Eğer gelirsen*, not *Eğer gelirsin*. And *ne zaman* with `-sA` means **whenever**; for **when** in a statement, use `-(y)IncA` or `-DIğIndA` ([B1 unit 7](gp-ince), [B1 unit 8](gp-diginda)).

blocks.title: Whatever happens
blocks.text: A conditional followed by the same verb in the third-person imperative means **no matter what**: *Ne olursa olsun* (whatever happens), *Kim gelirse gelsin* (whoever comes). That pattern comes in [B2 unit 1](gp-wh-ever).

sections.title: Gitsen iyi olur: advice and suggestions

blocks.text: A handful of everyday patterns use the plain `-sA` of the first section to advise, suggest and ask permission. They are softer than the imperative and the optative.

head: Pattern
Example
Meaning
rows: `-sA` + *daha iyi olur*: it would be better
It would be better to take the bus.
Is it all right if I open the window?
`-sAn?` with a rising voice: why don't you?
Why don't you rest a bit?

blocks.text: **You'd better.** *Gitsen iyi olur* is friendly advice, softer than *gitmelisin* ([A2 unit 6](gp-meli)). In the negative: *Bunu ona söylemesen iyi olur* (You'd better not tell him). *Daha iyi olur* compares two options.

**Shall we?** *Gitsek mi?* is more tentative than *Gidelim mi?* ([A2 unit 7](gp-optative)): the speaker is thinking aloud, and *acaba* makes it more so: *Bu akşam dışarı çıksak mı acaba?* (I wonder if we should go out tonight).

**May I?** `-sAm olur mu?` asks permission, a little more gently than `-(y)Abilir miyim?`: *Burada otursam olur mu?* (Is it all right if I sit here?). Typical answers are *Tabii, buyurun* and *Maalesef olmaz*.
**Why don't you…?** A bare `-sA` with the voice rising, often with *bir* or *biraz*, is a gentle suggestion: *Ona bir mesaj atsan?* (Why don't you send her a message?).

items.tr: Şemsiye alsan iyi olur, yağmur yağacakmış.
items.seg: Şemsiye al|sa|n iyi olur, yağmur yağacakmış.
items.en: You'd better take an umbrella; they say it's going to rain.
Shall we leave early tomorrow?
Is it all right if I sit here?
Why don't you send her a message?
You'd better not tell him that.

lines.en: What should we do at the weekend?
If the weather's nice, let's go to the sea.

lines.tr: O zaman sinemaya gideriz. Nasıl istersen.
lines.en: Then we'll go to the cinema. Whatever you like.

lines.tr: Tamam. Annemi de çağırsam olur mu?
lines.en: OK. Is it all right if I invite my mother too?
Of course! I'd be really glad if she came.

summary: `-sA` + type II endings is the conditional: *gelsem, gelsen, gelse, gelsek, gelseniz, gelseler*; negative *gelmesem*; question *gelsem mi?* (should I come?).
Alone, `-sA` imagines (*Param olsa alırım*), wonders (*Ne yapsam?*) and suggests (*Biraz dinlensen?*).
For a real condition, add `-(y)sA` to a tense: *gelirsem, gelmezsem, geliyorsam, geldiysem, geleceksem, gelmişsem*; for the future, use the aorist: *yağarsa*.
Nouns and adjectives take `-(y)sA` too: *hastaysan, evdeyse, varsa, yoksa, değilse*; *yoksa* also means **otherwise**, and *yarın vaktin olursa* puts *var* in the future.
*Eğer* can open the clause but never replaces the suffix; *Ya … -sA?* asks **what if**.
A question word + `-(I)rsA` gives **whenever, wherever, whatever**: *ne zaman istersen, nereye istersen, ne istersen*.
Advice and suggestions: *Gitsen iyi olur* (you'd better), *Gitsek mi?* (shall we?), *Otursam olur mu?* (may I?).
